key_insight: The paper turns short-range-order alloy design into a differentiable optimization problem, enabling direct gradient-based search from a target SRO pattern to a target material property.
engineering_relevance: This provides a faster, scalable route for property-driven alloy design, reducing trial-and-error in multi-principal-element alloy development.
method: Replace random-swap reverse Monte Carlo with continuous atom-occupancy variables optimized by gradient descent.
Add a physics-based correction term to keep designed structures thermodynamically realistic across many elements.
Train a small neural network to map composition and SRO statistics to mechanical properties, closing the design loop.
evidence_signal: Across nine FCC and BCC alloys, the pipeline reproduced SRO-driven stiffness changes from -20% to +57%, was faster and more accurate on 4000-atom systems, and matched 3 of 4 Co-Cr-Ni target stiffness values within 6%.
watch_item: Results depend on sufficiently large simulation cells; the paper reports that 108-atom cells can give misleading stiffness trends, with at least 864 atoms needed for reliable direction and magnitude.
paper_title: Differentiable inverse design of short-range order in high-entropy alloys: from target sro to target property
